metadata.title: Students’ reading enjoyment as a multilevel mediator of the relationship between parental reading enjoyment, teachers’ stimulation of reading, ICT factors, and reading literacy
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata restricted to South Korea (15-year-old students) with students nested in schools, and it applies the sampling weight provided in the PISA dataset to account for the complex sampling design. The analytic sample comprises 6,650 students from 188 schools, and the model is estimated with multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM) to respect the hierarchical structure. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that PISA sampling weights were applied. Replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not mentioned, and the analysis instead relies on Mplus estimation and Monte Carlo confidence intervals for mediation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of publicly available PISA 2018 data, restricted to South Korea only. The study analyzes reading literacy as the primary domain using the ten plausible values provided by PISA for students in South Korea, and it uses student and school questionnaires (including the optional teacher questionnaire for teacher self-efficacy). The analytic sample is described as 6,650 students from 188 schools; the paper does not specify additional exclusions beyond the multilevel FIML handling of missing values.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (South Korea, student level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MSEM path coefficients (unstandardized B): PER→SER B=0.430 (p<.001); ICT interest→SER B=-0.119 (p<.001); PER→Reading literacy B=10.079 (p=.007); ICT interest→Reading literacy B=36.109 (p<.001); SER→Reading literacy B=42.753 (p<.001). Model fit: Student level RMSEA=0.070, CFI=0.871, TLI=0.840, SRMR=0.046.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading literacy data for South Korea, the study leveraged Parents’ reading enjoyment, Students’ ICT interest, and Students’ reading enjoyment (plus controls such as Gender and ICT competency) to model reading literacy, finding that higher parental reading enjoyment and higher student reading enjoyment were associated with higher reading literacy, while higher student ICT interest was associated with lower reading enjoyment and (indirectly) lower reading literacy. This indicates that strengthening home reading culture and fostering students’ reading enjoyment may be more effective for improving reading literacy than focusing solely on ICT engagement, though the study is cross-sectional and mediation cannot establish long-term causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (South Korea, school level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MSEM path coefficients (unstandardized B): TSR→SER B=0.144 (p<.001); SIC→Reading literacy B=-16.064 (p=.015); TE→Reading literacy B=2.018 (p=.949); SER→Reading literacy B=346.304 (p=.005). Model fit: School level RMSEA=0.071, CFI=0.927, TLI=0.912, SRMR=0.110.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading literacy data for South Korea, the study leveraged Teachers’ stimulation of reading, Schools’ ICT capacity, and Teachers’ instructional self-efficacy (with Students’ reading enjoyment and ESCS as key components) to predict reading literacy, finding that teachers’ stimulation of reading increased students’ reading enjoyment which in turn related to higher reading literacy, while schools’ ICT capacity had a significant negative direct association with reading literacy. This indicates that school-level interventions should prioritize classroom practices that directly stimulate reading and build enjoyment, and that simply increasing school ICT resources may not improve literacy without effective instructional guidance.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 reading literacy data for South Korea (6,650 students from 188 schools) and estimates a multilevel structural equation model (MSEM) to test how reading enjoyment mediates relationships among parental, teacher, and ICT-related factors. Reading literacy is modeled using the ten PISA plausible values, and the analysis applies PISA sampling weights to address the complex sampling design. At the student level, parents’ reading enjoyment and students’ reading enjoyment are positively associated with reading literacy (e.g., SER→Reading literacy B=42.753, p<.001), while students’ ICT interest is negatively associated with reading enjoyment (ICT interest→SER B=-0.119, p<.001) and shows a significant direct association with reading literacy (ICT interest→Reading literacy B=36.109, p<.001). At the school level, teachers’ stimulation of reading increases reading enjoyment (TSR→SER B=0.144, p<.001) and enjoyment predicts reading literacy (SER→Reading literacy B=346.304, p=.005), whereas schools’ ICT capacity has a significant negative direct effect on reading literacy (B=-16.064, p=.015). Limitations include cross-sectional mediation (no long-term causal inference) and the absence of ML predictive modeling despite the paper’s ML-related framing in the introduction.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an empirical multilevel mediation study using MSEM (SEM framework) rather than machine-learning prediction/classification. Consequently, no ML algorithms are evaluated, so ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and ml_techniques.primary is null. The extraction focuses on the structural relationships and mediation effects reported in the Results tables, which are not ML model performance metrics.
